passage:
People keep asking me why I've gone quiet at work. So here it is. I'm Tejas, Mehr's husband of two years, and last Tuesday a bank letter came to the flat addressed to her.

I opened it by mistake. It was a repayment notice. For a loan I'd never heard of. A big one.

When she came home, she went white. She said it was for her brother Asif, for his shop, eight months ago. She'd been paying it quietly every month.

I remember standing in the kitchen feeling like the whole building had tipped. And then this hot, burning feeling: I'm the fool here. Everyone knew but me? Did Asif know I didn't know?

The worst part came that night. Lying awake, I started going through everything. The new phone she said was a gift. The weekend at her mother's. What else?

qa.q: Who was the loan for?
qa.a: The loan was for Mehr's brother Asif, for his shop.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: He felt shocked and humiliated, a burning sense of being made a fool, followed by doubt about what else was hidden.

qa.q: What could help Tejas at this raw stage?
qa.a: He could avoid big decisions for a few days and tell Mehr he needs the whole story, calmly, rather than questioning every past memory alone at night.

qa.q: How might Mehr have felt when she saw the letter was opened?
qa.a: Mehr likely felt panic and shame, knowing the secret she had kept for eight months was out.

grounding: A husband discovers his wife hid a large loan for her brother and feels shock, humiliation and a sudden doubt about everything else.

passage:
Even now, I can hear my own voice in that argument, and I wince. I'm Parveen, and I'd hidden a loan from my husband, Salim, for almost a year.

The money was for my brother Noor, whose small printing press was about to close. Abbu was ill; there was no one else. I knew Salim thought Noor was careless. I pictured his face, the lecture, the "no." So I signed the papers alone.

When Salim found out, I felt sick with shame. But instead of saying that, I heard myself shouting, "You would never have agreed! You never help my family!"

I saw it land. His face closed. I'd turned his hurt into his fault.

I was torn in half that night: between Noor, who I couldn't abandon, and Salim, whom I'd lied to. And too scared to say which part of me was right.

qa.q: What was the money for?
qa.a: It was for Parveen's brother Noor, whose small printing press was about to close.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when shouting 'You would never have agreed!'?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and afraid, and defended herself by attacking, which deepened Salim's hurt.

qa.q: What could Parveen say instead that might open repair?
qa.a: She could name the shame directly: 'I was scared you'd say no, so I hid it, and that was wrong,' without blaming Salim.

qa.q: How is Salim affected by Parveen's defence?
qa.a: Salim is hurt further, since the blame shifts onto him just when he needed the lie acknowledged.

grounding: A wife torn between family loyalty and fear of her husband's anger hid a loan and now defends herself in a way that adds to his hurt.

passage:
Sunday, late

I checked the bank app four times today. Jasleen doesn't know. Or maybe she does.

It's been six weeks since I found out about the loan. She's told me everything, I think. She cries when she talks about it. And still I look at her face when her phone buzzes, trying to read it. When she said she'd be late from the office on Thursday, I felt my stomach drop, and I asked three questions in a row like a policeman.

She said quietly, "Jatin, I feel like I'm living with a detective." She's right. I hate it too.

It isn't that I want to punish her. I think my mind is trying to make sure nothing surprises me like that again. But I'm so tired. I'm her husband, not her guard.

Maybe it's time to talk to someone about this. Both of us.

qa.q: How many times did Jatin check the bank app today?
qa.a: He checked it four times.

qa.q: What is Jatin feeling after six weeks of checking?
qa.a: He is exhausted and anxious, afraid of another shock, and unhappy about acting like a guard.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Jatin now?
qa.a: He could tell Jasleen honestly about the checking and suggest they see a counsellor together, as he is already considering.

qa.q: How does Jasleen experience Jatin's watchfulness?
qa.a: Jasleen feels watched rather than forgiven, as if living with a detective.

grounding: A husband keeps checking accounts and reading his wife's face after a hidden loan, which exhausts him and makes her feel watched.

passage:
Raghav,

You asked me twice last week, and both times I told you part of it. I'm not doing that again. Here is all of it, in one place, so nothing else surprises you.

The loan was for Leela, for her college fees. I took it in March. I didn't tell you in March, or in June when I took a second, smaller one because the first wasn't enough. That second loan is the part I left out on Tuesday. I'm sorry.

I've attached every paper: the agreements, the statements, the repayments so far. There is nothing else. If you find something I've missed, it's because I've forgotten, not because I'm hiding it, and I'll tell you the moment I remember.

I'm not going to say "but it was for family." Hiding it was wrong. It was my choice and I own it. You're my husband, and you deserved to hear it from me first.

Your wife,
Nirmala

qa.q: When did Nirmala take the second loan?
qa.a: She took the second, smaller one in June.

qa.q: What was Nirmala probably feeling while writing this letter?
qa.a: She seems ashamed but determined, wanting to finally be fully honest so Raghav stops being surprised.

qa.q: Why does one complete account matter so much at this stage?
qa.a: Trust can't be rebuilt while new facts keep appearing; putting everything in one place lets Raghav stop bracing for the next surprise.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel reading about the second loan?
qa.a: Raghav may feel a fresh sting of hurt, but also some relief that he finally has the whole picture.

grounding: A letter shows a wife telling everything at once and plainly owning that hiding it was wrong, so rebuilding can begin.

passage:
Dear Uma,

You asked how Zorama and I are doing after the loan business. Better, slowly. I wanted to tell you what we set up, because it's helping.

Every Sunday evening we sit with tea and both our phones and go through our accounts together. His and mine. That was important to me; I didn't want it to feel like a punishment only for me.

We also agreed on a family rule. If either of our families asks for help, we talk about it together before anyone says yes or no. If we can't agree, we sleep on it and ask Pu Lalthanga, our pastor, to sit with us.

We said we'd do the Sunday reviews for six months and then decide together whether to keep them.

Some Sundays are awkward. But last week Zorama laughed at my coffee spending instead of frowning. That felt like something.

Love,
Lalremsiami

qa.q: When do Lalremsiami and Zorama review their accounts?
qa.a: They review them every Sunday evening.

qa.q: What does the laugh last Sunday suggest about how Lalremsiami feels?
qa.a: It suggests Lalremsiami feels hopeful and relieved, seeing Zorama relaxing enough to joke.

qa.q: Why does it help that the routine includes both partners' accounts?
qa.a: It makes the openness mutual, so it feels like a shared reset rather than a punishment, and gives one partner safety and the other a way to show change.

qa.q: How might Zorama feel during these Sunday reviews?
qa.a: Zorama likely feels safer knowing nothing is hidden, and over time more able to relax, as the laugh suggests.

grounding: A letter describes a couple sharing visibility on accounts and agreeing how to decide on family help, with the routine mutual and time-limited.

passage:
March: Sudha met Damini for lunch. Damini was smiling for the first time in weeks. "Kunal and I went to the beach. He held my hand. I think we're okay." Sudha was glad, but careful not to say "so it's over."

April: Sudha stopped by with mangoes and found Damini red-eyed. A letter from the bank had come, a routine one, and Kunal had gone silent for a whole day. "I thought we'd moved past it," Damini said. Sudha sat beside her. "Maybe it's not backwards. Maybe healing is just bumpy."

June: Over coffee, Damini said the bad days were fewer, but they still came. Sudha said gently, "If it keeps flaring up, a counsellor might help you both talk about it without reopening everything." Damini nodded slowly. "Kunal said the same thing last week."

qa.q: What did Sudha bring in April?
qa.a: She brought mangoes.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she saw Damini smiling in March?
qa.a: Sudha felt glad and relieved, but also cautious, not wanting to declare the problem finished.

qa.q: What did Sudha offer that could help the couple?
qa.a: Patience with setbacks and the idea of seeing a counsellor if the hurt keeps flaring, so they can talk safely.

qa.q: What is it like for Damini when a routine bank letter sets things back?
qa.a: Damini feels discouraged and hurt, afraid their progress has been lost when the old memory flares.

grounding: Over several months a friend sees trust return unevenly, urges patience with setbacks and suggests a counsellor if the hurt does not ease.

passage:
On the first day after the summer holidays, Class 5 got new seats, and Zainab found herself next to Deepak, a boy she'd barely spoken to.

During the maths period, a cricket card slid out of his pencil box. A bowler, the rare kind with a gold edge.

Zainab gasped. "You have that one?"

Deepak's eyes went wide. "You collect?"

By lunch, they had both tins open on the bench under the stairs. She had three batsmen he didn't have. He had two keepers she needed. They argued happily over who was faster, then traded.

The next day Deepak saved her a seat on the bus. The day after, they made up a joke about their maths teacher's moustache and couldn't stop laughing.

Neither knew the other's birthday yet. It didn't matter.

qa.q: What fell out of Deepak's pencil box?
qa.a: A cricket card fell out, a bowler with a gold edge.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she saw the card?
qa.a: She felt excited and curious, thrilled to find someone who shared her hobby.

qa.q: What small things helped the friendship grow?
qa.a: Sitting together, trading cards and sharing a joke gave them easy reasons to spend time together.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when he saves Zainab a seat on the bus?
qa.a: Deepak probably feels happy to have a new friend and wants to keep sharing time with her.

grounding: In school, two children seated together discover a shared love of cricket cards, and friendship grows from the bench and jokes.

passage:
Tuesday: At lunch Uma broke her mango bar in half and gave one piece to Sachin, who had forgotten his tiffin. She watched to see if he'd say thanks or just grab it. He said, "Thanks, you're a lifesaver," and grinned.

Thursday: During art, Uma whispered, "I'm scared of the dark. I still sleep with a night light." Then she held her breath. If he laughed, she'd say she was joking. Sachin didn't laugh. "I sleep with my old teddy," he whispered back. "Don't tell."

Monday: A boy teased Uma about her braces. Sachin said, "Leave it." At break, Uma told Sachin about her fight with her cousin. She'd never told anyone that before. He listened and didn't tell a soul.

qa.q: What did Uma share with Sachin on Tuesday?
qa.a: She shared half of her mango bar.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she whispered her secret on Thursday?
qa.a: She was nervous, holding her breath and afraid Sachin might laugh.

qa.q: What helped Uma trust Sachin more each time?
qa.a: Sachin reacted kindly: thanking her, sharing his own secret instead of laughing, and keeping her story private.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel when Uma tells him about her cousin?
qa.a: Sachin probably feels trusted and proud to be a friend she can confide in.

grounding: Over several days two children share snacks and secrets, quietly checking whether each act of trust is kept safe.

passage:
Simran, when I was ten, like you, my best friend was Pushpa. Your Kalyani Nani will tell you how that felt.

We walked home together every day by the canal. We had a secret code: one knock on the desk meant "meet me at the gate", two meant "the teacher is coming".

Oh, it was joy. Every morning I ran to school to see her.

But one day at recess, Pushpa played kho-kho with the new girl from Pune. Just once. I stood by the water tap and felt something hot and hurt in my chest. I wanted to shout, "She's MY friend!"

I didn't speak to Pushpa all afternoon. On the walk home, she knocked on my slate twice and laughed. I laughed too, and it passed. But I remember that first sting.

qa.q: What did one knock on the desk mean?
qa.a: One knock meant "meet me at the gate."

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling at the water tap?
qa.a: She felt hurt and jealous, as if Pushpa belonged only to her.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped the hurt pass?
qa.a: Pushpa knocking twice and laughing on the walk home, and Kalyani laughing back instead of staying silent, let them move on.

qa.q: How might Pushpa have felt when Kalyani didn't speak to her?
qa.a: Pushpa may have felt confused, since she only played once with the new girl, but she reached out playfully.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood best friendship with codes and walks home, its joy and possessiveness, and the first hurt at recess.

passage:
From the staff room window of her school in Jayanagar, Mrs Rao watched the lunch break the way she always did.

Last year, Aditi and Elizabeth had been inseparable, two heads bent over one sketchbook. This term, Aditi had joined the football team. Now she ran across the field with a pack of shouting players while Elizabeth sat with the art crowd under the gulmohar tree, painting.

Mrs Rao noticed that Elizabeth looked up whenever the football group ran past. Once, Aditi waved. Elizabeth waved back and returned to her painting.

In class, they still sat near each other, but they talked less.

Mrs Rao felt a small ache, remembering her own school friends. Nobody had done anything wrong. It was simply the new term, pulling each of them towards something she loved.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth sit with the art crowd?
qa.a: She sat under the gulmohar tree.

qa.q: What was Mrs Rao feeling as she watched the two girls?
qa.a: Mrs Rao felt a small, wistful ache, remembering her own school friends drifting apart.

qa.q: How could Mrs Rao support both girls without forcing anything?
qa.a: She could give them a chance to work together in a class project now and then, while letting each enjoy her new group.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when the football group runs past?
qa.a: Elizabeth may feel a little left behind or wistful, glancing up but still enjoying her painting.

grounding: A teacher notices two once-close children drifting into football and art groups, with no one at fault.
